Scores 1–5: 1 severe mismatch, 2 material problems, 3 usable with reservations, 4 good, 5 unusually strong. samples.brief: A customer and a shopkeeper misunderstand which parcel belongs to whom.

content.title: Dos paquetes
content.story:
Ana entra en una tienda. Hay dos paquetes sobre la mesa.

—Hola. Soy Ana. ¿Está aquí mi paquete?

El vendedor toma el paquete grande.

—Sí. Este paquete es de Ana.

Ana mira el paquete.

—¿Este paquete es de Luis? Mi paquete es pequeño.

—¿Usted no es la madre de Luis? —pregunta el vendedor.

—No. Soy Ana Pérez.

El vendedor mira la etiqueta del paquete grande. En la etiqueta hay un nombre: Luis Pérez.

—Ah, este paquete es de Luis Pérez. Perdón.

El vendedor toma el paquete pequeño. Ana mira la etiqueta.

—Aquí está mi nombre: Ana Pérez. Este paquete es mío.

El vendedor le da el paquete pequeño.

—Gracias —dice Ana.

Ana mira una foto en la mesa. En la foto hay una taza azul.

—¿Hay una taza como esta en la tienda?

—Sí —dice el vendedor—. Las tazas están aquí.

Ana camina con el vendedor. Ana lleva su paquete pequeño.

glossary.meaning: To enter or go into. “Entra” is the present form for Ana.
In or on; shows location, such as in the shop or on the table.
A or an. “Una” accompanies feminine nouns; “un” accompanies masculine nouns.
Shop or store.
“Hay” means there is or there are; the same form works for one or several things.
Two.
Parcel or package. “Paquetes” is plural.
On or on top of, describing the packages on the table.
The. “El” accompanies masculine singular nouns, “la” feminine singular nouns, and “Las” feminine plural nouns.
Table.
Hello; a greeting.
To be, used here for identity and ownership. “Soy” means I am; “es” means is, including with polite “usted.”
To be in a location. “Está” and “está” refer to one package; “están” refers to several cups.
Here, in this place.
My; placed before a noun. “Mi” is capitalized at the start of a sentence.
Seller or shopkeeper; the masculine form used for the person serving Ana.
To take or pick up a package. “Toma” is the present form for the shopkeeper.
Large or big; describes the package.
Yes; an affirmative answer. The accent distinguishes it from “si,” meaning if.
This. “Este” accompanies masculine “paquete”; “esta” refers to the feminine noun “taza.”
Of or belonging to; links a package to its owner or a mother to her child.
To look at. “Mira” is the present form for Ana or the shopkeeper.
Small; the masculine singular ending agrees with “paquete.”
You, in polite singular address. It takes a third-person verb form, as in “Usted ... es.”
No or not; rejects a statement or makes it negative.
Mother.
To ask a question. “Pregunta” is the present form for the shopkeeper.
Label attached to a package.
Of the; the required combination of “de” and masculine singular “el.” Here it links the label to the package.
Name; the name written on the label identifies the package's owner.
Ah; expresses realization when the shopkeeper notices the mistake.
Sorry; a brief apology for the mistake.
Mine; expresses ownership without repeating the owner's name. The masculine singular form agrees with “paquete.”
To her, referring to Ana in the sentence where the shopkeeper gives her the package.
To give. “Da” is the present form for the shopkeeper.
Thank you.
To say. “Dice” is the present form used for Ana and the shopkeeper.
Photo or photograph. It is feminine: “una foto.”
Cup or mug. “Tazas” is plural.
Blue; describes the cup.
Like this one; Ana asks for a cup similar to the one in the photo. “Esta” refers to the feminine noun “taza.”
To walk. “Camina” is the present form for Ana.
With; indicates that Ana walks together with the shopkeeper.
To carry or take along. “Lleva” describes Ana carrying her package.
Her here; identifies the package as Ana's. It agrees with the singular thing possessed, not with the owner's gender.

content.title: Dos paquetes
content.story:
Ana entra en la tienda. El vendedor tiene dos paquetes sobre la mesa. Un paquete es grande. El otro paquete es pequeño.

—Hola. Soy Ana. Busco mi paquete —dice Ana.

El vendedor toma el paquete grande.

—Hola, Ana. Este paquete es de Ana.

Ana mira el paquete.

—¿Este paquete es de Ana? Mi paquete es pequeño.

—Este paquete tiene un libro —dice el vendedor.

—Mi paquete también tiene un libro —dice Ana—. Pero este paquete no es de Ana.

El vendedor mira el nombre en el paquete grande.

—Ah, el nombre es «Ada». ¡No es «Ana»! El paquete grande es de Ada.

Ana mira el paquete pequeño. El nombre está en un papel blanco.

—Aquí dice «Ana» —dice Ana.

—Sí. El paquete pequeño es de Ana —dice el vendedor.

El vendedor da el paquete pequeño a Ana. Ana abre el paquete. Hay un libro azul.

—Este es mi libro. Gracias.

Ana mira una foto en el libro. En la foto está la tienda.

—¿Por qué hay una foto de esta tienda?

El vendedor mira la foto.

glossary.meaning: Parcel or package.
Shop or store.
Seller or shopkeeper.
To look for. «Busco mi paquete» means “I am looking for my package.”
Name.
To belong to someone. «El paquete grande es de Ada» means “The large package belongs to Ada.”
Placed before the verb to make a negative statement: «no es de Ana» means “does not belong to Ana.”
Small.
Here.
Why?
forms: ¿Por qué hay una foto de esta tienda?

materialIssues: “¿Usted no es la madre de Luis?” introduces a negative identity question and a family relationship into the ownership mix-up, increasing inference demands despite otherwise simple clauses.

“El vendedor le da el paquete pequeño” and “Este paquete es mío” introduce an indirect-object pronoun and a possessive pronoun; both are accurately supported, but add grammatical load relative to the guide's preference for explicit references.
“Ana camina con el vendedor. Ana lleva su paquete pequeño.” leaves the shopping activity open, but the cup question has already been answered; the continuing thread is natural yet narratively weak.
strengths: Concrete objects, present-tense clauses and repeated names make the parcel correction easy to follow.
All supplied notes have sound contextual meanings and form explanations, including “del,” “le,” “mío,” “su” and feminine “foto.”
Broad support covers common words as well as potentially less familiar expressions without relying on note count alone.
Agreement and regional neutrality are maintained.

materialIssues: “¿Este paquete es de Ana?” and “Pero este paquete no es de Ana.” make Ana repeatedly refer to herself by name. This is understandable as deliberate clarification, but noticeably less natural than “¿Este paquete es mío?” and “no es mío.”
“El otro paquete” and “Mi paquete también tiene un libro” introduce contrast and addition without definitions; these useful expressions deserve support under the learner's broad-definition request.
“¿Por qué hay una foto de esta tienda?” is an accessible but more demanding reason question. The “¿por qué?” note explains why, but leaves “hay,” “foto” and demonstrative “esta” unsupported.
“El vendedor da el paquete pequeño a Ana. Ana abre el paquete.” contains important action verbs absent from the glossary; sparse support also leaves much of the basic narration unexplained.
strengths: The Ana/Ada label confusion provides a concrete, coherent explanation for the parcel mistake.
All ten notes are contextually accurate; the phrase-based forms provide useful examples.
The unexpected photograph grows directly out of the delivered book and creates a clear, natural unresolved question.
Short clauses, repeated nouns and correct agreement generally support the A1 brief.
